extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing nature writers and literary readers interested in nature writing
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writers composing nature essays or creative nonfiction about the natural world, focused on how to balance factual detail with lyrical reflection and respect for place-based knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness and factual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature writing should include specific, concrete particulars about the natural world (e.g., how eagles hold their wings flat, when wheat ripens, where a species nests) rather than relying on vague, generalized language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts saying an eagle 'soars' with noting its wing posture; warns that writing that 'turns aside from detail' can feel 'unmoored, and adrift.' Anti-pattern: calling something 'pretty' or evoking emotion without grounding in observable fact, which risks vacuousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of facts and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong nature writing marries the external assembly of names and facts with internal feeling and reflection, letting both modes occur simultaneously rather than forcing an either/or.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote from Richard Smith: there's 'less conflict than I had imagined' between factual and emotional modes; exemplary writers (Annie Dillard, Robert MacFarlane, Barry Lopez, Diane Ackerman) teach readers about nature and about themselves. Aim to unite concrete description and philosophical or emotional insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for place-based and indigenous knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 'whats and wheres' of places—the names and concrete facts embedded in local/indigenous knowledge—as genuine ways of mapping and knowing a landscape, acknowledging their complexity and relationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inuit knowledge binds facts about fox travel, fishing places, and nesting sites within networks of relationship and memory. Don't romanticize or appropriate: acknowledge sources, avoid making assumptions about practices you haven't observed firsthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obsessive cataloging without insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Cataloging species, photographing, and listing facts without articulating the accompanying insight reduces writing to mere inventory and can fail to convey meaning or wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of the 'sticklers' who 'forget to articulate the insight that accompanied those facts.' Guidance: present facts but also explain why they matter or what they signify in human and ecological terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of metaphor and anthropomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors and anthropomorphic language can illuminate relationships between people and nature but should be used carefully so they inform rather than misrepresent biological realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion of Robin Wall Kimmerer: some readers find talk of moss's 'generosity' destabilizing, while the author defends metaphor's utility. Use analogy/figurative language that reveals meaning, but be mindful of not making unwarranted claims about conscious intent in nonhuman life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of motive and avoiding self-indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear whether the piece aims to teach about the natural world or to use nature as a mirror for personal exploration; using nature merely as a prompt for self-expression can read as self-indulgent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes two tendencies—writing to understand oneself versus writing to teach about nature—and warns that motive and temperament dictate form. Aim for balance so personal reflection does not eclipse factual or ecological content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainspoken, flowing language; avoid overwrought prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be accessible and flowing rather than forced or excessively flowery; overwrought prose can obscure the writer's message and lose readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Susan's complaint: writers 'try to outdo each other with forced or overly flowery language' or veer off on 'cognitive side trail[s] that hurt my brain.' Strive for prose that 'flows over me and pulls me along' without obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate evocative facts into field/guide writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Even practical identification guides and place guides benefit from occasional vivid, illustrative facts or analogies that help readers notice and remember features of the landscape or species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example desired aside: describing volcanic pumice as 'foam on a glass of soda' to make a floating rock notable. Anti-pattern: guides that contain only dry facts (e.g., 'South Rim campground has sixty full-service RV sites') without moments that capture wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance urgency of cataloging with depth of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of ecological crisis, the impulse to catalog and preserve knowledge is understandable, but writers should balance this urgency with efforts to convey deeper meaning, practical knowledge, and wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes some writers 'are frantically cataloging to preserve knowledge before it is too late' yet argues 'we need everything at once: facts, meaning, practical knowledge, wonder.' Avoid letting urgency reduce pieces to mere lists of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation and technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Good nature writing often derives from careful empirical observation and learning technical details (timing, behavior, habitat) that anchor evocative language in real-world knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between scientific/empirical writers (who note planting times, species' habits) and abstract writers; recommendation: learn and include technical particulars to give your writing a firm foundation.
